cvEn:
Eyal Niv, son of Ruth and Michael, was born on 1 Shevat 5713 (17 January 1953) in Rehovot. He attended the "Revivim" elementary school in Kiryat Haim and continued at the military boarding school attached to the Reali School in Haifa.

Eyal was a member of the youth movement HaNoar HaOved VeHalomed (the Working and Studying Youth). He loved to hike the paths of the country, and in his photographs he captured his close bond with the land and its landscapes.

He was an enthusiastic athlete and took part in basketball, athletics and high jump, and won first place several times.

Eyal enlisted in the IDF in mid-March 1971 and volunteered to serve in the Air Force. When he was accepted to the flight course, he began as a pilot cadet, climbing slowly and laboriously through the first stages of the advancement ladder. Eyal loved flying and enjoyed his studies on the course and getting to know this new dimension. But only after his first solo flight in the Fouga training aircraft did it become clear that he was not suited to be a pilot. His commander then wrote to his parents: "Eyal did not succeed as a pilot, but it is important that you know there is no connection between the assessment of flying ability and the assessment of a person as a person."

Eyal was part of every group he joined, deeply attached to his friends and family members, who loved him dearly. He was liked and admired by children. He was distinguished by his good judgment, his deep understanding, his cheerfulness and his good nature. He was remarkable for his dedication and his readiness to help anyone.

On 27 Sivan 5732 (9 June 1972), in the week when he was due to decide on the continuation of his path in the IDF, Eyal was killed in a road accident. He was laid to rest in the military cemetery in Haifa.

The commander of the flight school wrote to his family that Eyal "was a good friend, a young man whom his comrades valued, a person other young men wanted to be near." His direct commander wrote in a letter of condolence to his parents: "Eyal was a quiet, thoughtful and likable young man, who was loved by both trainees and commanders alike."
